Averting a Crisis

By: Michael Duffett | Production

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
A state of emergency had been called in response to the dire water shortage in the w cape. New restrictions are in place, but unless the wc govt and council can come up with quick additional water supplies there is a god possibility of our taps running dry. We take a brief look at what projects there are in the pipeline – but they are years away to implement. What can be done within the next 6 months to avert a disaster. We paint a dooms day scenario what happens to a city when the taps run dry, we ask the city to explain if they have a disaster plan ready should the taps run dry. But most important we ask why the city has not considered desalination – there are 15 000 desalination plants around the world and they are literally saving cities, and countries like Saudi Arabia. One cape Town company has the answer – they are involved consulting in 16 other countries and can get a plant up and running within 4 months, and add capacity. And at no cost to the city. This company pays for all the infrastructure and will sell the water for between R11 and R15 per 1000 Litres. The present going rate is between R7 and R30 dependent on the amount of water used by homes and businesses.

There are desalination plants in south Africa. Some of dead ducks, like the one that was put into Lamberts bay for a huge cost, by a French consortium. It’s never produced one cup of water. Others are underperforming. Middle people are making huge profits.

Press Release:


Cape drought
Western Cape dam levels have dropped to a critical 18% and with no sign of winter rain to bring much-needed relief, the province has been declared a disaster area.
Emergency plans are hurriedly being put into place to supplement existing water supplies, while long-term solutions are being sought. The city has meanwhile urged
residents to only use water for absolute essentials, but consumption still remains way above target levels. Carte Blanche asks: will the disaster declaration result in swift
action or is it too little too late?

Script:


Divers here are clearing debris from the lowest inlets at western cape dams to allow for the extraction of every last drop of water……

Borehole drilling companies are struggling to keep up with the demand in cape town as home owners, businesses and sports clubs scramble for their services, in response to the worsening drought.

Gabby de Wet: In the last couple of months we've been clocking about 200 plus phone calls a day. Impossible to deal with all of the enquiries. This is not even the online enquiries via our website.

With an estimated half billion rand already suffered by the wine industry, farmers throughout the western cape are holding their breath.

Marinus: At this stage if we have a below average or an average rainfall we will be in dire straights next year.

And all over cape town billboards are displaying alerts. It is crisis time.


These images tell the story. Currently the average dam levels are sitting at about 19 per cent of which ten per is unusable. In this footage you can see where the level once was.

Link: It's only when you come to one of the dams that you fully appreciate the full extent of the water crisis. This is the Theewaterskloof, one of the feeder dams for the city of cape town and its currently at 13% capacity and what’s even more frightening is not all of that is available for consumption.

Theewaterkloof is so low that the pumping station became stranded and a canal had to be dug to allow water to reach it.

Expected rains over the last two months have not made landfall because of high pressure systems diverting it elsewhere.

Kevin Winter: We have obviously been massively disappointed that theses high pressure systems have been going south and we not quite sure as to why that is happening. It is obviously driven by a global system.

Water scientist Dr Kevin Winter is a worried man.

John: People are now talking about day zero: That’s quite disconcerting.
Kevin: Yes, so I think that that brings about a very powerful impact. Whether we are going down hat route, it is a scenario at any rate. I think that we going to as I have said before squeak through.

Winter Rain is expected but again, there again there is no certainty. Mayor Patricia De Ville said last week said that if the rains don’t come cape town will face a crisis of catastrophic proportions.

(Up sound)

No wonder capetonians are turning to prayer – and recently the mayor attended a multi faith prayer meeting and addressed the clergy on the slopes of Table Mountain

(up sound)

Mayco member Xanthea Limberg says that the city is prepared for the worst case scenario.

Xanthea: Firstly, lifeline supply will entail tankers being provided across the city to provide access to municipal clean drinking water for essential purposes.
JOHN: When do these contingency plans kick in?
Xanthea: Well we will be sending out those or putting into effect those contingency measures when we reach the below 5% mark,

Kevin: Well its a scenario that we really don’t want to contemplate and I think one has to recognize that its a scenario at any rate. There are countries and whole regions that have experienced complete lack of water, taps have run dry and that’s pandemonium in lots of ways.


Link: Last month western cape premier Helen zille declared the province a disaster area as it tried to deal with its worst water crisis in more than 100 years. But many critics are saying that its a step that should have been taken far sooner.



In the hot seat is western cape premier Helen Zille who like others has been left perplexed by weather patterns

Zille: I keep on asking the forecasters why are your predictions so wrong and they say well climate change is making prediction all the more difficult

John: Some people feel that the province has dropped the ball on this crisis.

Zille: Well the bottom line is this. You don’t start working on a crisis on the day of the announcement. We’ve been working on this crisis for many years. And in fact tried to get the declaration at the end of 2015 when it was refused but we have continued working flat out although within the constraints required by law and regulation.
John: What was it about the month of may that made you declare the province a disaster area?

Zille: Well there was nothing specific about the month of may except that that is when we got permission from the national disaster management center to do so

With the threats of taps running dry in just three months, the province initiated a project called Avoiding Day Zero. It allows for the freeing up funds to fast rack projects which were scheduled for years down the line.

Zille: Currently we are talking about 300 million in process to do that and the reprioritizing of our budgets to achiever that. We are appointing hydrologists across the province to identify the best places to drill boreholes.

There is a major aquifer in the southern cape called the Table Mountain group aquifer. Billions of liters of water lie trapped in the sandstone. there is only one place like this in the world and that’s in south America.

Chris Hartnady: We don’t get these things everywhere. We have got this opportunity. You know we should relish what we have.

Earlier this year we described the work of dr Hartnady and Umvoto, a consulting company who has been working with the city exploring the possibity of drilling for this water deep down in the earth.

Chris Hartnady: Drilling into rocks which are almost pure quartz, its on Moahs Hardness scale. Its up at 8 just below topaz and corundum and diamonds.
John: So very hard?
Chris: That means very hard and very strong.

The drilling was only scheduled for 2024 but now that has all changed. Umvoto and a drilling company will start work within a month. Deep bore holes will be dug next to three dams where existing water delivery infrastructures already exist. An initial yield of 3 million liters per day is forecast but this will be up scaled. Though on a smaller scale in terms of population size to cape town, Hermanus which suffered a crippling drought several years ago makes use of this aquifer after Dr hartnady and his team struck water after drilling to over 200 meters. The aquifer supplies a third of the town’s potable water needs.

LINK: The famous line by Samuel Coleridge "Water, water everywhere nor not a drop to drink" is especially pertinent in Cape Town today. It is a city enveloped by two oceans and yet it is only now that this extraordinary resource is going to be taken advantage of.

Desalination was in the city’s long term planning but it has now been fast tracked to augment the water supply. It makes sense. Some countries like Saudi Arabia, with little or no rainfall, would be in trouble without desalination. A local Somerset west companies ground breaking technologies is being used there as well as in 15 other countries. It says it can install and maintain at its own cost modular systems which can provide the city a 100 million liters per day within four months. It would however charge the city between R11 and R14 per 1000 liters, more than what consumers pay the metro.

Julius steyn: We proposing a modular process which is mobile, or semi mobile and semi permanent installations. That means if we are lucky that the rains come within the next three years and that all the dams are overflowing, well then that modular system can be relocated to other parts of the world or the country where it is required.


The city is however paying a R100 million rand to another company to install two modular systems at and close by the Koeberg power station. They will provide at this stage 5 million liters per day. But some of the new accelerated water supply schemes are months if not years away. At this stage the cities target is a limit of 500 million liters per day.

And that’s why stage 4 water restrictions were introduced last week. It prohibits any irrigation with municipal dirking water and encourages an overall consumption of a 100 liters per person per day to prevent the taps running dry.

Zille: Well that thought keeps me awake at night. It really does and it keeps me washing myself with an old fashioned vaslap and a small bowl of water most days of the week. So it has changed my behavior and will change my behavior permanently.


The city maintains that the only way to get through the drought is to reduce water consumption. In all their rate bills and on social media, they are providing tips on water saving.

Xanthea: We are trying to break down that 100 liters per person per day and in the recent communication that we have done we have indicated that please do not shower for more than 2 minutes. Don’t flush the toilet more than 5 times a day because all of those things combined will push you over that 100litre threshold.

Zille: The most important thing we have to do in dealing with this crisis was to change people’s attitudes to water. Just like 4 or 5 years ago we had to change people’s attitudes to electricity. South Africans thing water is a free resource. And there is nothing like a good crisis to make people understand that they have to fix the leak in their toilet. That they can’t leave taps dripping


While boreholes are being drilled at vulnerable places like hospitals to prepare for the worst, it seems there may be a glimmer of hope on the horizon for a huge storm is predicted for this coming week, with 80 millimeters or rain expected.

One thing is for sure, there is a lesson for cape town and south Africa. Because of climate change and resulting complex weather patters, we should never take surface water for granted again.

Kevin: I think that this is a sufficient warning about our reliance and over reliance on surface water to change the projection for our water resources forever. We cannot go back to where we were before. WE cannot continue to rely on surface water as we have been doing.
